title: Kenya DPA defines 'consent' as express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed
claim: The Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 defines consent as any manifestation of express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed indication of the data subject's wishes.
evidence_summary: Section 2 of the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 provides a statutory definition of consent requiring express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed indication of the data subject's wishes by statement or clear affirmative action.
source_excerpt: "consent" means any manifestation of express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed indication of the data subject's wishes by a statement or by a clear affirmative action, signifying agreement to the processing of personal data.
interpretation: The statutory definition imposes a high, consent-opt-in standard: consent must be express and informed, and cannot be inferred from inaction.
citation: Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019), s.2 (Kenya Gazette Supplement No. 181), s.2.
methodology_or_basis: Direct quote from the primary legal text (section 2, interpretation).
notes: Real corpus record. Text extracted from acquired PDF (source_id=12); locator page 6.

title: Kenya DPA grants data subjects enumerated rights
claim: The Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 grants data subjects rights to be informed, to access, to object, to correction and to deletion of personal data.
evidence_summary: Section 26 of the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 enumerates data subject rights including information, access, objection, correction and deletion of personal data.
source_excerpt: 26. A data subject has a right — (a) to be informed of the use to which their personal data is to be put; (b) to access their personal data in custody of data controller or data processor; (c) to object to the processing of all or part of their personal data; (d) to correction of false or misleading data; and (e) to deletion of false or misleading data about them.
interpretation: The Act codifies individual data-subject rights enforceable against controllers, indicating a rights-based approach to data governance.
methodology_or_basis: Direct quote from the primary legal text (section 26).
keywords: data subject rights, Kenya, access, correction, deletion
notes: Real corpus record. Text extracted from acquired PDF (source_id=12); locator page 19.

title: Fayda ID consent-based participation per NIDP legal framework
claim: The World Bank ID4D report states that Ethiopia's legal framework for Fayda digital ID requires individual consent before any authentication processed by the system, with a signed consent form at registration.
evidence_summary: A 2024 World Bank ID4D study on Fayda ID reports that the legal framework stipulates individuals, as owners of their personal data, must give consent before authentication, and sign a consent form before registration explaining data use.
source_excerpt: Implement a consent-based participation and data exchange in Fayda ID. The legal framework stipulates that the individual, as the owner of any personal data collected for the digital identification system, must give consent before any authentication processed by the system. Individuals sign a consent form before registration that explains how their data will be used.
interpretation: This documents the consent architecture as legally required in the Fayda framework. It is a statement about the legal framework, not evidence of effective consent practice in the field.
citation: World Bank ID4D, 'End-user perspectives on Fayda ID from marginalized and vulnerable groups' (2024), p.29.
methodology_or_basis: Qualitative study; direct quote from report findings/recommendations section.
relevant_policy_or_law: Ethiopian Digital Identification Proclamation No. 1284/2023 (as referenced)
notes: Real corpus record. Text extracted from acquired PDF (source_id=9); locator page 29.

title: UNECA: no comprehensive Ethiopian personal data protection law as of early 2024
publisher_or_author: United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
claim: As of early 2024, Ethiopia lacked a comprehensive personal data protection framework and a delegated supervisory authority, with a draft data protection proclamation awaiting parliamentary approval.
evidence_summary: UNECA's 2024 country profile states Ethiopia was not signatory to the AU Malabo Convention, had no comprehensive personal data protection legal framework or delegated oversight authority, and that a draft personal data protection proclamation had been submitted to parliament awaiting approval.
source_excerpt: Without a comprehensive legal framework for personal data protection or a government authority delegated with oversight, companies are free to manage data as they see fit... However, a draft proclamation on protection of personal data has been submitted to parliament and is waiting approval.
interpretation: Documents the pre-2024 legal gap. Note: this reflects the state as of the report date (early 2024); the Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024 was gazetted 24 July 2024, after this report. This evidence does not support claims about the post-2024 legal state.
citation: UNECA, 'Digital Trade Country Profile: Ethiopia' (2024), pp.8-9.
methodology_or_basis: Institutional country profile; direct quotes from report pages 8-9.
relevant_policy_or_law: Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024 (later law)
keywords: data protection, Ethiopia, UNECA, legal framework
notes: Real corpus record. Text extracted from acquired PDF (source_id=10); locators pages 8-9.
